title: Ignoring a String method's result
summary: Why calling a String method may leave your text unchanged, and how to keep the new result.
objectives: Explain that a Java `String` cannot be changed after it is created.
Trace what happens when a `String` method returns a new value that is not saved.
Fix code by assigning a method's result back to a variable.
Spot the same mistake with methods such as `trim`, `replace`, `substring` and `concat`.

blocks.text: You call `toUpperCase()` because you want a name in capital letters. But the name stays the same. This is a common beginner mistake: the method returns the new text, and the program throws that result away.

bad.title: The returned text is ignored

good.title: Save the returned text

blocks.note: Both programs compile and run. Java does not reject the first program: calling a method and ignoring its result is allowed. The mistake shows up when the program runs, because `name` still holds `Ada`. Assigning the result back to `name` fixes it.

blocks.text: A `String` is immutable. That means its text cannot be changed after it is created. A method such as `toUpperCase()` makes and returns a new `String`; it does not edit the old one. If you do not save the returned `String`, it is discarded.

blocks.caption: What happens when you call name.toUpperCase() without an assignment
blocks.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A[ name holds Ada ] --> B[ Call toUpperCase ]
  B --> C[ Return a new String ADA ]
  C --> D[ Result is discarded ]
  A --> E[ name still holds Ada ]

blocks.caption: String[] words = {"cat"};
blocks.name: words
blocks.note: The same idea applies to an array element. `words[0].toUpperCase()` returns `CAT`, but does not replace `words[0]`. To update the array, assign the result: `words[0] = words[0].toUpperCase();`.

blocks.title: Keep the result
blocks.text: When a `String` method returns text you want to keep, assign it to a variable. Often that means writing `name = name.methodName();`.

blocks.text: The key question is: where is the returned text stored? In this code, nowhere. With `name = name.toUpperCase();`, the new text is assigned to `name`, so the next print uses `MIRA`.
The fix is to save the result of the method call. Here are two methods that return new `String` values.

bad.title: The trimmed result is ignored

good.title: Assign the trimmed result

blocks.note: `trim()` returns text with the outside spaces removed. It does not change `label` itself. The bad program therefore prints the original length, `7`; the good program saves the trimmed text and prints `3`.

blocks.text: The method name changes, but the reasoning stays the same. If a `String` method returns new text, a bare call does not update the old `String`.

blocks.note: `replace()` returns new text. Without the assignment, `message` still holds `red car`.
`substring()` returns a new `String` containing the selected part. Save that result if you want `word` to hold it.
`concat()` returns a new `String`; it does not add text to the existing `greeting`.

blocks.explanation: `trim()` returns a new `String`. Assigning it back with `title = title.trim();` makes `title` hold the trimmed text.

blocks.explanation: `replace()` returns `fun`, but the result is not assigned. The variable `word` still holds `sun`.

items: A Java `String` is immutable: its text cannot be changed after it is created.
Methods such as `toUpperCase()` and `trim()` return new `String` values.
A method call such as `name.toUpperCase();` compiles, but its returned text is discarded if you do not save it.
Assign a result back when you want the variable to hold the new text: `name = name.toUpperCase();`.
Use the same reasoning for `replace()`, `substring()` and `concat()`.
